To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the phenotypic variance in the trait is partitioned into additive, dominance, and epistatic components; (2) the additive genetic variance is partitioned into components due to the additive effects of the loci and to their interaction with each other; and (3) the epistatic variance is partitioned in an analogous manner to the additive variance, with the additional complication that epistatic effects can be of the additive or dominance types.

the genetic basis of phenotypic variation in the number of spines in a single spine cluster is not constant throughout the life cycle, but changes over time, and that the genetic basis for this change is not due to a change in gene expression, but is due to a change of the genetic architecture of the trait, i.e. the genetic basis of the trait is not the same in the two life stages.
